titleText.es: ¿PENSÁIS QUE ESTO ES COSA DE BROMA?
titleText.en: DO YOU ALL THINK THIS IS A JOKE?
titleText.noteEn: Pensáis is the informal plural “you” form used mainly in Spain.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone asks another person to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of pedir, then que, then a special requested-action form of the other verb.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish calls that special form the subjunctive. It shows that the action is requested rather than stated as a fact. For example, viene means “comes,” but venga is the requested form in pedir que venga. The form after que changes for the person who is supposed to act.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you introduce an explanation, excuse, or hesitant objection?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Start with es que, then give the explanation.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Es que often softens what comes next, especially when the speaker is explaining a problem or pushing back politely. The phrase functions as a unit; its meaning is not obtained by translating es and que separately.

example.es: No puedo ir; es que trabajo esta tarde.
example.en: I can't go; the thing is, I work this afternoon.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is more of a certain quality than another?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put más before the describing word and que before the other thing.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The describing word is an adjective, such as alto for “tall” or importante for “important.” Más raises the degree, and que introduces what you compare it with.

example.es: Este libro es más corto que aquel.
example.en: This book is shorter than that one.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you reject further objections with “no buts”?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pero normally means “but.” Spanish can turn it into the plural noun peros for objections or excuses, so sin peros literally treats those “buts” as things that are not allowed.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: ser cuestión de vida o muerte
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is a matter of life and death?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ser followed by cuestión de vida o muerte.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cuestión de introduces what kind of matter is at stake. Vida o muerte is a fixed contrast used for an extremely serious or urgent situation.

example.es: Para ellos, es cuestión de vida o muerte.
example.en: For them, it is a matter of life and death.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you refer to the highest speed something can reach?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Punta often means a point or tip, but after velocidad it forms the established technical combination velocidad punta. Máxima velocidad is another way to express a maximum speed.

example.es: El tren alcanza su velocidad punta.
example.en: The train reaches its top speed.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone suddenly starts running?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of echar or echarse, then a, then correr.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In this expression, echar does not keep its usual sense of throwing. The whole pattern marks the sudden beginning of running. Both echar a correr and echarse a correr are used.

example.es: Al oír el ruido, Pablo echó a correr.
example.en: When Pablo heard the noise, he started running.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that an action is done to someone or something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then the verb's completed-action form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish calls that completed-action form a past participle, often ending in -ado or -ido. In this passive pattern it changes to match the person or thing: atrapado for one masculine person, atrapada for one feminine person, and plural forms ending in -ados or -adas.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you connect a fact to its consequence with “so” or “which is why”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use por lo que before the consequence.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Por lo que looks back at the fact just mentioned and introduces what follows from it. The three words work together as one result connector.

example.es: Perdí el autobús, por lo que llegué tarde.
example.en: I missed the bus, which is why I arrived late.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is restricted to a particular amount or option?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use estar, then limitado or limitada to match the thing, then a before the limit.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Limitado changes to agree with the thing being described: limitado for a masculine singular noun and limitada for a feminine singular noun. Only estar changes for person and time; a introduces what the restriction allows.

example.es: La entrada está limitada a dos personas.
example.en: Entry is limited to two people.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you label a drawing whose sizes are not in their true proportions?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Write no a escala, meaning “not to scale.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A escala says that the dimensions follow a fixed proportion. Adding no warns that lengths and distances in the drawing should not be compared literally.

example.es: Este mapa no está a escala.
example.en: This map is not to scale.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you introduce an assumption with “assuming that…”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use suponiendo que before the assumption.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Suponiendo que sets a condition or fact that the speaker temporarily accepts for the discussion or calculation. It can introduce either a realistic working assumption or a hypothetical one; the verb form after que depends on how the assumption is presented.

example.es: Suponiendo que llega a tiempo, empezamos a las ocho.
example.en: Assuming that she arrives on time, we start at eight.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say how long someone takes to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of tardar, the amount of time, en, and the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Tardar changes for who takes the time. En links the time to the action and normally has no separate English word in this pattern.

example.en: I take ten minutes to arrive.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that an amount is cut or divided in half?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use por la mitad after the verb.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mitad means “half.” With verbs such as dividir, reducir, or cortar, por la mitad says that the result consists of two equal parts; it is understood as “in half,” not as a literal instruction to divide by one-half.

example.es: Cortó la manzana por la mitad.
example.en: She cut the apple in half.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: Velocity describes motion; acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A speed can be measured in meters per second. An acceleration in meters per second squared says how much that speed changes each second.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: a triangle with three equal sides and three equal 60-degree angles
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Because all three sides and angles match, an equilateral triangle is symmetric around its center. That symmetry matters in distance and path problems.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: the comic turns an ordinary math exam into planning for a velociraptor attack
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The joke treats kinematics, geometry, route planning, and the movie-like danger of clever raptors as urgently practical school material.
